title: A Grove rate limit is a continuously replenishing bucket, so maxAmount caps instantaneous exposure while slope caps sustained throughput
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.3.1 gives the whole mechanism in four lines:

```
return _min(d.slope * (block.timestamp - d.lastUpdated) + d.lastAmount, d.maxAmount);
```

Capacity accrues linearly in real time at `slope` units per second from whatever was left after the last use, and is clipped at `maxAmount`. There is no window, no epoch and no reset — which matters, because period-based limits are gameable at boundaries (spend the whole budget at 23:59 and again at 00:01) and produce a sawtooth exposure profile.

The two parameters answer two different questions. `maxAmount` bounds how much can happen **at one instant**, which is the size of the worst single incident. `slope` bounds how much can happen **per unit time**, which is how fast an adversary or a malfunctioning relayer can drain a position while humans notice and respond.

Their ratio is a third, implicit parameter: `maxAmount / slope` is the time to refill from empty. The Atlas's own instance configurations show it being tuned deliberately — the Centrifuge JTRSY inflow (A...3.1.1.1.2.4.1) is 500,000,000 USDC max with a 500,000,000-per-day slope, a one-day refill, while Centrifuge JAAA (A...3.1.1.2.2.4.1) is 100,000,000 max with a 50,000,000-per-day slope, a two-day refill. The second counterparty gets both a smaller cap and a slower recovery.

A...1.3 also states the governance duty attached: limits "must be maintained in line with Grove's strategy, market conditions, and security considerations" — they are living parameters, not set-and-forget constants.
description: getCurrentRateLimit returns min(slope * elapsed + lastAmount, maxAmount), regenerating capacity every second rather than resetting at period boundaries.
